utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I call Nikola Petrovic. NIKOLA PETROVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that will be handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Nikola Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Nikola Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you come from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Novi Sad and I live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your occupation in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Banja Luka I have been a policeman for 15 years. Before that I was in restaurant business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Dusko's brother somewhat longer than Dusko and I met Dusko sometime in 1974, '75.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which brother of Dusko's have you known for a longer period of time than Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubo Tadic is -- Ljubomir Tadic is the one whom I have known longer than Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How well did you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rather well, because at certain points in time we socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know other people in the Tadic family, for instance, his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him only once when I paid him a visit in Kozarac as he was still alive then and I had heard that he was quite an eminent personality in Kozarac. They lived in Kozarac after World War II. I know his mother, and I know all four brothers and their wives. I know the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you used to visit the Tadic family in their home in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kozarac I visited the home when I was younger and some time on the eve of the war, sometime in 1992, I would drop by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when the conflict started in Kozarac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time of that conflict in Kozarac, whereabouts were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Banja Luka doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you a married man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I have three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your home is in Banja Luka, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We have a family house in Banja Luka, but I am now using an apartment. Yes, that is where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict in Kozarac, were you in your former family home or in the apartment where you now live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home in this house that my family has because at that time I still had not been given the lease to that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict in Kozarac, did you see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict I did, before the conflict, but when the war started I did not see him, and later on I used to see him in Banja Luka later, some two, two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if Serb people were moving out of Kozarac before that conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know that, but Dusko moved out or, rather, his mother and I think his wife and children left a few days earlier, and on the eve of the conflict Dusko escaped, fled from Kozarac because unrest had begun there and he had to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The time that you saw the mother and the wife of Dusko Tadic and the children before the conflict, can you remember how long before the conflict that you saw those members of the Tadic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 10 to 15 days, I cannot remember exactly when that was, but when I would come from Kozarac I would go to the birth place of my father, that is Sanski Most, and then on returning I would drop by to see Dusko and they were all there. We were in Dusko's coffee bar, the one that he had, and we had a few drinks there. I saw his mother. Then we went upstairs in his house and we were their guests because our wives, that is Dusko's wife and my wife, were school fellows, and there was a gentleman there, I believe it was an Orthodox priest there who just happened to be there at the time. So I saw his mother there, his wife, his two children. He lived with them. That was their common household.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember how long before the conflict this was when you went to the coffee bar on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 10 or 15 days. I cannot remember exactly. It was a period of time. I mean, it was quite a long time ago and I attached no importance to it. I did not know that it would suddenly come to mean a significant date or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the last time you saw the Tadic family as a family in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the last time in Kozarac, yes. On that occasion Dusko told me, I saw the glass piece broken on the coffee bar. I mean, they had been stoned. So we talked and I learned that he had some difficulties with those local Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you next see the Tadic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tadic family, except mother, mother did not come to visit me, and mother was with one of his brothers, and as for them I saw them on the very day when the conflict broke out in Kozarac. I believe that was that day, Dusko came to see me with his children. It must have been sometime in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what day that was, what the date of that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a weekend and I should say that it was May 24th or 23rd, I cannot really say exactly. But, at any rate, those were the days of weekend in May. I cannot remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You first of all told us about seeing the Tadic family for the last time in Kozarac at the coffee bar about 15 days before the conflict started. Had you seen them in Banja Luka at all in that period of 15 days before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic with his family at the time of the start of the conflict, had you seen him in Banja Luka before that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic at the time of the conflict, had you seen him at all in Banja Luka in the days before the conflict started in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic then at the time of the conflict in Kozarac, can you remember precisely who in his family was with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, when they came to visit you, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His wife and his two children were with him in my home when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what the reason for seeing you in your home was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was a close friend of his and he had nowhere to run to, and he came to Banja Luka because I lived there and his brothers lived there and he was looking for accommodation. He had to find some accommodation because he could not go there as there were armed conflicts there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long did you see Dusko and his family on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this occasion, you mean that day or in the days ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, when you saw him at the time of the conflict and you said that he and his family visited your home, how long did they stay at the home for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they spent with us the whole afternoon. We sat there. My wife prepared lunch and told me, "Go and get some bread" because, of course, we know what our daily needs are, and since there were four persons more she told me to go and get some bread, and I went to a restaurant nearby and bought some bread so that they could have something to eat. So they stayed until the -- until evening, until dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic again after that time in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I used to see him in the days that followed every two or three days. We met regularly because he was looking for a way out, how to resolve this problem that he had, what to do. He did not know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the problem that he had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the problem at the time to begin with, he was concerned about the property he had, that he had left behind. That is this coffee bar. I knew that he had rescued some of his effects before the conflict, but he was concerned about this property. Then he came to Banja Luka, that is, to the centre of the town where we met or he visited me at my home. He had financial problems because one has to have some means of livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he have a job at all in Banja Luka after he arrived there during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not do anything. He was with his brothers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say you saw him every two or three days. Do you know whereabouts he was living at this time in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not visit them, but I think he rented a house, but I did not visit that house. I could not offer him any hospitality because I lived with my two parents who later on died, but there was no room at my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how long the Tadic family stayed in Banja Luka for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said about two, two and a half months they were around since they fled from Kozarac, and then later on he went to Prijedor when raids started for men of military age who were to go to the front, and some of them did not want to go to the front and he also refused to go to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was Dusko Tadic mobilized, as far as you knew, at this time of the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do know that he was not mobilized. I can vouchsafe that, but later on he had to respond to mobilization because, of course, when military police arrest you without your mobilization documents, they immediately take you to the front line, to a place where you do not want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that Dusko Tadic went to Prijedor. Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when he left Banja Luka, I can -- I am telling you I cannot remember all those dates exactly, but after Banja Luka he went to Prijedor and I think he reported to the traffic police because that was his mobilize -- the place where he was mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the reason then he went to Prijedor because of his mobilization for the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I think they provided him with some provisional accommodation, that is, accommodation for his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic as a character, do you know if he was heavily involved in nationalist politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that, but I know that later on when he left the police, then he was given the post of a Secretary of a Local Commune but that was after the conflict was over. He became a Secretary of a Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before that time had he expressed extreme nationalist views to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice anything of that kind. In that regard he was quite restrained and he was saying: "This cannot end well". He did not like the situation. He did not believe that a war of such a scale would break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he moved to Prijedor did you see him during that period of time that he was living in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him in a flat, I think it was at Pecani. I would not know exactly which flat that was. He took me with his brother and I saw his mother and wife and the two children. They were in that apartment, and he also had his brother's son there, I think, spending the weekend with them, I believe, a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is Pecani a place where there are apartment blocks in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, it is a residential -- it is a new development area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that that you saw him in the apartment in Prijedor? Can you put a date on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know the date, but I saw him when he was the Secretary of the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for you visiting Dusko Tadic in Prijedor at the time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply had asked his brother, was Dule, "How about Dule?" I simply wanted to see where he was and how they had been accommodated. I remember it was Sunday, it was a weekend, so I could have a day off and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the sort of gap in time, can you remember that, the period of time, since you had last seen him when you saw him in the apartment in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was several months, but I cannot remember how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After that period of time, did you see Dusko Tadic again in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came to Banja Luka and told us he was going to Germany because there was nothing for him there. There was no work. He had no money, and he offered to sell me his music appliances, the gramophone, the radio and everything, to sell it to me, because he had no money. I cannot remember what was the price he asked, but I also had no money to buy it, and then I think he went to his brothers and somehow managed with the money and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know when that was? Are you able to perhaps be precise about that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat, it was several months after my visit in Pecani in Prijedor. It was two or three months. I cannot remember exactly because it was a long time. It was four years ago, but I do know that he did not go along with -- get along well with Prijedor authorities. That is what I do know. He had to leave. He wanted to leave. I have a sister living in South Africa -- she has been living there since 1990 -- and he asked me to give him her telephone number and her address, because he was thinking to go there. Even I thought of leaving Banja Luka but I could not leave my parents who were of an advanced age. I have already told you. I mean, they were of quite an advanced age and their health was poor. And he talked to her and she explained the procedure, I mean, what were the requirements to enter South Africa, but it was simpler for him to go to Germany because he had a brother who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that he had problems with the authorities in Prijedor. Do you know what those problems were, did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did say something, that he could not agree with certain things. I would not know exactly what about; that they were sending them to the front line and then requesting him to put on the SMB uniform, that is, to stop being with the civilian police and that was when he then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask, but wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, did Dule Tadic leave for Germany in 1992, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was in '92 or '93. I think it was '93. It has been a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just calculating it because you said that it was a couple of months, you thought, after you had seen him in Prijedor, in the flat in Prijedor. So from calculating from that, do you think it is probably 1992 or '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in that apartment for several months, but then he was not given a permanent lease to that apartment. He had to leave the apartment at one point and as he was due to leave, the apartment was probably returned to somebody else and he had difficulties with the authorities, and then that obviously made his decision to leave. Exactly how long that all took, I cannot remember exactly. I do not know the date, but I do know that there were several months elapsing before the decision and the actual departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said you were in the police, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the police attached to the prison service, the prison service police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Were you active in the police during the period of the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not in 1992. In 1995 I was mobilized on two occasions, because our boss was asked to send the names of so many people to form a unit and I was called up in the winter of 1995 as the Commander of a supply unit and in the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you doing in 1992 in the months of, say, May, June and July of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was in our prison service, that was, I was doing my routine jobs. This was the Banja Luka prison headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. This is a civilian type prison, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a civilian type prison. This is a civilian prison with a section which was for military detainees because the military prison was full so they sent some people to us in that military prison unit for those serving shorter sentences, and we provided the services of guarding and security for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the prison service Tunjice, Banja Luka. This is both the prison and the district prison, local and district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does the prison have a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, special name, Tunjice, Tunjice was the name by which it was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say there was military prisoners there as well during the period of the conflict, were they people who were serving in the armed forces or were they people who were brought in, civilians who were brought in, and taken as prisoners during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were people who were -- some of them wanted to destroy the bridge on the Una River, so they were caught by the military police. This was the case of people who were captured, and they were sent to us simply to be guarded there because they had no room in their own prison. This was the territory controlled at that time by the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these people Muslims, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, Croats. There were some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st March 1959 and I was born at Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the day of the conflict commencing in Kozarac, you say that is the day you remember seeing the Tadic family, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that the conflict had started in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that -- I mean, the first information came from Dusko who came to visit. This was the first real information that I know. The distance is not very great. It is less than 40, 42 kilometres between Banja Luka and Kozarac. So there were people who were travelling and moving between, coming from the various villages in the vicinity of Kozarac. So we got the information from them about the clashes and conflict in Kozarac and around Prijedor. The media did not report these conflicts for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it is, basically, relying on information as people were coming in, as refugees were coming through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not refugees, but various people who worked in Banja Luka and were coming from the various villages in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The tensions built up, did they not, in the Kozarac and Prijedor opstina over a period of time? It just did not sort of happen overnight? I think you need to answer "yes" or "no", sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, not overnight, certainly not. It took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: People were coming and going during this build up period before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The conflict was somewhat spasmodic, was it not, in the sense that it did not all begin on one day; it started at various places at different times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conflict in and around Kozarac and Prijedor (and they are very close, just 10 to 15 kilometres distance), it started in one place and then it spread as wild fire and it simply spread including more and more villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you are not denying, are you, that there was -- you may not know, but if you do know, you are not denying that there were conflicts in other places at different times in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of other conflicts, but I know that only this one conflict broke out in that place along the main road linking Banja Luka and Prijedor. There was a member of the Territorial Unit, a Muslim, killed a soldier of the Yugoslav Army, which was then the Yugoslav Army, and that is how the whole thing started. This was the focal point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You know that because someone told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that from several people, but they -- all the stories agreed and that is the relative truth that I have developed myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the Tadic family arrived at your house, how did they arrive there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said in your evidence that, as far as you know, they had just arrived, is that correct, the family had just arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came on foot to me, but the mother, wife and children, they -- the mother was sent to live with his brothers, and they came to me in the afternoon hours to visit my family home which was not very far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that, so far as you know, the first day that they arrived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Dusko, yes, but for the wife and children, I concluded from what they told me that they had arrived earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that you visited the house in Kozarac at sometime prior to the conflict commencing; I think you said, was it, 10 to 15 days before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the conflict, probably that period of 10 to 15 days I visited their family house. I was on my way from Sanski Most because my father's -- my father comes from around Sanski Most. I went to visit some uncles and some relatives there, and as I was returning I was passing on the main road, some kilometre or two kilometres from the house, so it was on my way and I came to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any constraints on travel at that time or were you able to freely drive along the roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not travel very freely, no. I left the main road and I was met by the Territorial Unit of Kozarac, the Territorial Defence Unit. At that time this was a self-styled Unit because the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina had not separated yet and the Muslims built their own units. They had an emplacement, machine gun emplacement. There were young people armed with karabins, with rifles, with automatic rifles. They had military blouses and jeans and tennis shoes and so on. For a Territorial Unit, they were rather funnily dressed, unusually dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there no armed Serbs around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that place there was a very small number of Serbs and the Serbs at that time were not armed. They had no checkpoints of their own. This was very early on, and the clashes began around Kozarac in Prijedor, Kozarac in fact, and it was only then that checkpoints started to be manned. The voluntary guards were in villages in the Croat, Serb, Muslim villages and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So there was no unrest or clashes anywhere else, anywhere in opstina Prijedor, prior to the commencement of the military activities in Kozarac, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Apart from Slavonia. Slavonia -- that is the Croatian territory, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I am talking about Prijedor itself, the opstina of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were mobilized who were leaving for Slavonia from the different communes and they were mostly Serbs. They were leaving for Croatia to fight there and they were mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So at this time there was a war going on in Croatia, was there, at the time you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw the broken window in Dule Tadic's shop premises, did he explain to you how this had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that a boy came to -- for provocation; because he was a Serb, Dusko was a Serb, he threw a stone. But Dusko, fearing wider unrest, did not do anything. He simply tried to calm down the situation and continued to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say what the ethnic background of this boy was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say whether he had any other problems with Muslims prior to this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me about this one problem. That was the only one which you could see, obviously, because the glass was broken as a result, and he said that most of the Muslims have stopped visiting his coffee shop, although some local Muslims were, indeed, still coming because he, Dusko, did not avoid socializing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it he was upset about the window of his shop being broken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, before the window was broken he showed no signs of unrest. After that again his initial rage at the damage and so on calmed down. So he was cool when he was explaining it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that you visited his flat in Prijedor, his apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Whose apartment was that prior to Tadic moving into it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I honestly do not know. I do not know. I know that he was given the use of the flat, but from whom he got it and whose it was, I just do not know. Sometimes people have a house and have a flat and it was against the rules to have both, so they would then ask somebody to take over the flat, simply to watch over it, to protect it, if you like. People are still doing that nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was a rather nice flat, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not specially luxurious, but it was, I think, a two-room apartment, nothing special, but this was enough for a family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it poorly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a bad apartment. This was a medium quality apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that you saw him a couple of times in Banja Luka after the initial visit when you first saw him, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What dates were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The dates were in the period of several days in an interval when I was free, when he was free, we could meet. My wife had a private business, so I was helping her in this business. So Dusko would come along often. We would have a drink together in a cafe and then on one occasion he showed me a newspaper, I think a Zagreb newspaper, where we could together read where it said: "Dusko Tadic, a war criminal". There was a big headline. The paper described massacre, rape and various other actions at which we simply laughed. This was incredible. This was just a lie, a big lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was published in Zagreb about the same time as you saw him ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Zagreb newspaper, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What, he had been indicted as a war criminal by this Tribunal, had he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That was before, before that. This was -- he was accused by the media, by the Muslim/Croat media. Somebody accused him like that and we read that as an article in the newspaper. It was not very clear because he was not even there, and if he himself had felt that he was a war criminal he would not have gone to Germany to ask for a job and live with his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But if he had known that people were claiming that he was a war criminal, he would have to be somewhat circumspect, would he not, in going to Germany or anywhere else outside the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he, of course, would have been more circumspect, but he never could believe that he would be arrested, that he would be brought to answer for these things because he felt he had not done that. Personally, as a friend of his, I think that it is impossible for him to have done such acts, and that is why I have agreed to come here and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me the crimes that he was accused of in this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he killed somebody called Karabasic, Karabasic I think was the name. Karabasic I knew personally and he was a weightlifter, and Dusko -- and then he was friends with the Tadic brothers who actually helped him to develop this particular sport in Kozarac, weightlifting. He was a short man, well built, with good muscles, and we, as a karate school, from his brother's club, we came and demonstrated karate and he demonstrated weightlifting to the young people of Kozarac. So, and also he brought some of his pupils and he -- and they demonstrated weightlifting. This was a rather primitive demonstration. This was back in 1977, I think, '78 perhaps. So he was, well, Dusko was in good relations and in both private and business with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. This article about the killing, the allegation that said that he had killed Karabasic, this was about May 1992, was it, the article that you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May or June, probably June, I would say. This was the time when he was in Banja Luka and this was probably early June. It was summer. I remember that we were sitting outside and having a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take part in the conflict in Kozarac at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, what is your ethnicity, what ethnic group do you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an Orthodox person, belonging to the Orthodox religion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb, well, Serbs are in Serbia. They are real genuine Serbs and we are Orthodox people in Bosnia and I was born in Serbia, but my origins are in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you consider yourself an Orthodox Christian, would that be your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The apartment that you visited where Mr. Tadic was living with his family in Banja Luka, you visited that apartment on several occasions, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, where he lived in the apartment -- you mean with his family in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go to that apartment, no.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Just in Prijedor was when you visited him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor and then Kozarac before the outbreak of the conflict and there I visited the apartments.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you never visited his apartment in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My tempo in life was much greater than his. I had to work hard. He had more time, so he would come and visit me. I did not visit him in that apartment. I do not know even know why I did not, but we used to meet in the town and I had no need to go to visit him in the apartment. His wife would come to my house and visit us, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know where he lived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Starcevica is a section, a district, in Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know the street, the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. Many of the street names have been changed in the meantime and those that had some kind of Muslim names, various popular heroes or writers. These have been changed now and there are Orthodox names now of people, Orthodox people, having the names in the streets.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Petrovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We would like him not to be excused at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you are subject to being recalled as a witness in this case. So you should make yourself available to the Tribunal. You should be in touch with Mr. Kay and Mr. Kay will tell you when and if you are needed to return to the Tribunal. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You mean today or in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, in the future. You are free to go home to Banja Luka now, but you should make yourself available to return. You may be asked to return to come to testify. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. You are now excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness is Borka Rakic, your Honour. BORKA RAKIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Borka Rakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts do you work as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the Chamber insists, I will answer that question -- must I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If no one else thinks it is important, perhaps I can pass over it ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- and maybe I can give an indication to the Prosecution over the short adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to know, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess at 11.30 so you can talk about it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a very long time. My sister is married to his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which brother is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko. My sister is married to his brother Dusko. I have known him for 15 years, if not longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us which of the Tadic brothers you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Mladen, I know Ljubo. My sister is married to Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other brothers, do you know any of the other brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko, yes, Stojan, yes. I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often have you seen Dusko Tadic in the past before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him seldom before the outbreak of the conflict in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you spend most of your time in Banja Luka where you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Tadic family home in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seldom, since I have to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the conflict occurring in Kozarac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic at all at the time of that conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that before the conflict or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know whereabouts the Tadic family were staying in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. They were staying in Koste Jarica Street which is a street which is some 10 minutes away from the street on which my mother lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could spell the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where Dusko stayed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: K-O-S-T-E J-A-R-I-C-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mention that because of the transcript. (To the witness): Do you know when the Tadic family came to stay in that house in Koste Jarica street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what the family consisted, what members of the family were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His mother, wife, two children and Dusko, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how long they stayed in that house for in Koste Jarica street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed there in May, June and part of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How far away from the house where they were staying was your parents' house which you said was nearby? Are you able to tell us in metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very close, about 10 minutes walk, perhaps less. They are small, short streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Tadic family in this house where they were staying at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know, for instance, how they obtained that property, how they came to live there? Do you know the circumstances how they came to be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the reason why he came, but personally I think that any man, regardless of his religion or his race, will flee his home if he feels threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to look at an exhibit now which is D62A, if that could be shown to the witness? (Handed) There is a photograph there in front of you, madam, of a house. Do you recognise that house at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this is the house that he stayed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if that could be put on the monitor? Can you tell us how often you went to that house when the Tadic family were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not often. I met him in the family circle with my mother's or at his brothers'.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you saw them at other places other than the house where they were staying in Koste Jarica Street, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know how long Dusko Tadic and his family stayed in Banja Luka for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was for about two, two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what Dusko Tadic was doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The occasions you have described seeing him and family gatherings, did you know why the family had come to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know the motive behind his coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic at this time, was he expressing any extreme nationalist views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know him to be an extremist in politics at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if Dusko Tadic remained living or staying with his family in Banja Luka at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time while he stayed there he did, but then he left for Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when that would have been when he left for Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask. That might be an appropriate moment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you, lawyers, resolve the issue that came up right before recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not be pressing the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Thank you. Mr. Kay, have you completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have concluded, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15th April'52.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background or nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am of an Orthodox religion and I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence-in-chief about the conflict in Kozarac. How did you come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In talking to friends in the street. In Banja Luka people talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did these people come from that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were people from Banja Luka, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But they did not tell you how they knew the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had a look at an exhibit, I think, that Mr. Kay showed you, Exhibit 62A. Might that Exhibit be put on the overhead projector and displayed, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could it be displayed on the screen? Madam, just looking at the photograph on the screen, can you tell me where you entered the building when you went to visit Mr. Tadic and his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came through the gate outside and they were living on the ground floor of this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In front of you there there is a silver type pointer, would you take that pointer in your hand and on the photograph itself, but not on the television screen, could you point to where you enter the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph].

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. How many floors of the house did they occupy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only one part, only one floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the one you are pointing to now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, have you been watching these proceedings on television, the proceedings of the trial of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you watch it regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have seen a number of the witnesses that have come and testified, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What part of the proceedings? You tell us. You tell us what parts you have seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it -- I saw it on Croatian radio and television, and they showed these proceedings temporarily from time to time only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You had discussions with Dule from time to time about his political views, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very often. We talked about normal, everyday things, not politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you never discussed politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence, and I think if I made a note of it correctly, that if people were threatened like him then it is to be expected that they would come to places like Banja Luka. I am not quoting it directly, but I think that is the effect of what you said, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the threat that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their lives were threatened, the lives of people were threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By anybody. If you find that your life is threatened, then it is normal that you should flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but do you understand who it was that was threatening them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The motives of his arrival in Banja Luka are unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us what those motives are then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: She said "unknown".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I thought you said "known".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said "unknown".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say you were aware of a threat, but you did not know what the nature of it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Rakic, did you see Dusko Tadic in Banja Luka then at the time of the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see him in Banja Luka after the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps the other microphone can be switched on as you are now facing towards me. After the conflict in Kozarac, did you see Dusko Tadic in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, what do you mean by at the time of the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to this witness being -- I am sorry, I forgot you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, two questions I wanted to ask you. The first one was, when you did see the accused was he wearing a uniform of any sort in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: He was dressed in civilian clothes, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him using a car at any time in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us what the quality of the accommodation was in the house in the picture where the Tadic family lived whilst they were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was not much comfort, not many conveniences. It was a basement flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to this witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, we would ask that the witness not be released at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You would ask that the witness ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not be released.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- not be released. OK. Mrs. Rakic, you are not being excused but it means that you still may return to your home, but you are subject to being recalled to the Tribunal to testify. So you should make yourself available, keep in touch with Mr. Kay, and if it is necessary for you to return, then you will be asked to return. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are now excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness is Miroslav Brdar. MIROSLAV BRDAR, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I read it out loud? I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Miroslav Brdar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your occupation, your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In what particular industry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Metal working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first meet Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we started to work on the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which checkpoint was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Orlovci, the checkpoint of Orlovci, six kilometres away from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that on the road between Prijedor and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time that you met Dusko Tadic and you worked at checkpoint Orlovci, were you in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the regular police or the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To work at the checkpoint, was that the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were your police headquarters based in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you first start working in the reserve traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediate -- just a few -- a short period of time before arriving at Orlovci checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was? Can you recollect the month of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the summer, summer, early July, three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you ever worked in the reserve traffic police before this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was working in the reserve traffic police part of your mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you worked at checkpoint Orlovci before Dusko Tadic came to work with you at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe two to three days before he arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the witness gave the date early July and then a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I am aware of that and further questions will be directed to that matter. [To the witness]: At the checkpoint Orlovci were you in a Unit of men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many men were in that Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three, three of us from the civilian police and two men from the military police, five people altogether. We, the civilian police, worked in our way and the military police worked on their own task but we occupied the same checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any police uniform that you wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me personally, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you describe that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an old uniform, the normal traffic police uniform that we used to have before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What colour was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Light grey. It was my uniform. That is what I wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You started to work at checkpoint Orlovci two or three days before Dusko Tadic joined you. Can you remember if the names of the people -- sorry, I will not ask that question because it will be confusing. The people that you worked with at checkpoint Orlovci before Dusko Tadic came to join you, did they remain working with you or did any of them leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were changes, there were changes. Some people were transferred to other checkpoints, I do not know why and for what reason, and they simply said that, "The three of you should remain here at the checkpoint Orlovci". The people who used to work with me before he arrived were then transferred to other checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Unit of three that you worked with, including Dusko Tadic, did that remain the same group of three people at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. Do you mean when Dusko arrived and worked with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the three of us remained, yes, Dusko Tadic, myself and Miroslav Cvijic. We worked together, the three of us. The three of us remained together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect for how long you worked together, the three of you, at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a couple of months, a bit more perhaps. I do not remember the dates, but I would say two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you all wear the same uniform or did you have different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember what uniform Dusko Tadic wore when he was at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he had a blouse, the camouflage uniforms, multi-coloured and he also had trousers to match but they were a bit paler, a bit lighter. The blouse was newer and the trousers, pants, were a bit older and, therefore, the colours were not as expressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other person in your Unit, Miroslav Cvijic, can you recollect what uniform he wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simple camouflage uniform, a bit newer and the colours were better, but we had to wear what we had. We could not have -- we could not choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at some documents from a book which have been supplied to the Prosecution in advance. Perhaps if you could look at this document?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before that document is presented to the witness, I would like to raise an objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is correct to say that that document was provided to the Prosecution in advance. However, in this case "in advance" means at 9 o'clock this morning. We have not had a chance to review the contents of that document. Incidentally, if I may, your Honour, enquire whether or not the witness speaks English? If he does not, I would ask that his headphones be removed during the course of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Brdar, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you take your earphones off, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We do not know the provenance of this document. We received previous documents, as the Court is aware, along with representations about their origin. I must presume that this document was not obtained at the same time and we cannot rely on those same representations because this document was not presented to us at that time. It was only presented this morning. In addition, I should note this is a rather severely redacted document. It is certainly difficult for that reason alone to decipher on its face and without sufficient time. We would like at least some opportunity to review it properly. We also are certainly going to need to know some more about that document before we can determine whether or not it is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay? Are you objecting on the grounds of authenticity or not sufficient time to examine, or what is the legal basis, not to be too technical?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think at this point, your Honour, both concerns exist. We have not had an opportunity to give it a proper review or even a sufficiently cursory review to satisfy ourselves that we can properly cross-examine or understand the direct examination of that document. Secondly, for the reasons expressed earlier, we are not in a position to waive any objections to its authenticity or foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can assist the Court? We delivered it last night with a translation. It is a document that recently came into our possession from the trip of the Defence team to opstina Prijedor in August of this year. If I had known there was to be an objection to it, I would, of course, have reshuffled my witnesses and this gentleman would have been called towards the end of the week so that the Prosecution would have had time to look at it and make their decisions. It is a document that comes from Prijedor police station. It was only to be given to us in a redacted form with a few general pages included within it. It is a document that details the shifts at checkpoint Orlovci from June until August 1992, including the Unit of three men that the Court has heard about in evidence this morning. As the Court knows, we have had three important witnesses removed from our schedule for this week who were originally to come here to the Court. The document would have been produced through them and they would have had intimate knowledge in relation to the production of the book. That being prevented by a third party caused us to have to rethink how to present this material. This is the only witness that I have presently who will be able to produce this material on behalf of the Defence. It is not a situation of our making. It is a situation that others have caused us to be in. It was originally intended, as I say, for other witnesses to present this material. But that course has been prevented. So this witness, who is aware of a number of background details, is the only means by which I can use this evidence which is important for the Defence alibi.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why did you not provide it to the Prosecutor earlier? You say you received it in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it has been translated and other documents as well were being translated. I cannot really answer why it was only served last night, but ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They are saying they have not had enough time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This witness, you estimate that he will require two and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do we not proceed and perhaps we can take an early recess? Let us see how far you can get into the testimony. Then that will at least give the Prosecutor over the noon recess to take a look at it ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and then see if he can prove it up. I do not know whether he will be able to prove it up or not in terms of its authenticity, but see what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us move along without it and then let us see what we can do over the noon recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The details concerning its production through this witness we only knew would be possible this morning because we have not seen him with the information. We did not know whether he was aware of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I am saying, perhaps over the recess you can talk with him and see whether he can prove them, establish their authenticity, how they were created and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I am grateful to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you put your earphones back on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you work the same shift at checkpoint Orlovci each day with Dusko Tadic and Miroslav Cvijic or did that shift vary?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I worked only with the two of them. We worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I am asking you about is, in fact, the time of day, the shift period. Was there more than one shift at checkpoint Orlovci during 24 hours or was there just the one shift?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: For one group, there was one shift, and if one day we had a day shift, the next day we had a night shift, and that was the change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you give the hours of those shifts that you used to work at checkpoint Orlovci? If you were on a morning shift, when would that start?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think, I cannot remember very well, but at 7.00, 7.00 or 8 o'clock in the morning, that would be the beginning. In the beginning, we worked shorter shifts, eight hours only. Later, because the situation was different, the shifts were extended and usually it was 10 to 12 hours. But the normal rotation was one day we had a day shift, then we had a night shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So at the start if you were on an eight hour shift, would there be three different shifts of different units during the day at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Later on, when it was extended to a 10 or 12-hour shift, did the shift pattern go down to only two units working at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think we had the same number of shifts, but if we worked longer, then we also were resting longer. It was too strenuous to work for the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand. Who was the leader of your shift of three of Cvijic, Tadic and yourself? Who was in command of the three of you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I would not call him the leader of the shift, but I was responsible in some sense. I was to bring the shift to the checkpoint, also to take it away from the checkpoint and to contact the station, the police station, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If perhaps now we could look at the routine of the shift? Before you started at checkpoint Orlovci, did you check in at Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Each time before we started, we were supposed to meet in front of the police station in Prijedor, and my two colleagues would be waiting in front. I would go inside and talk to the Commander of the police station. We were given the -- we were given the duty, list of duties, for that day and also the keys to the car to take us to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which Commander of the police station gave you your orders?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Djuro Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he the Commander of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think even now he is still on the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he in charge of the organisation of the traffic police from Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: He was. He was completely responsible for the traffic police. He was the Commander before the war, during the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He used to give you your orders. What sort of orders would they be before you started your shift?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, normally it was to check civilian traffic and civilian people driving the vehicles. That was all; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons with you when you were on checkpoint duty?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We had pistols and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The three of you had the same weaponry, did you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The pistol and automatic rifle that you were issued with, when were you given that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I received the automatic rifle from the civil police when I became a member of the police force in May. That was in early May when the authorities changed hands in Prijedor. As for the pistol, I had it from a person who was in traffic police before and it was my personal -- my personal pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described leaving the police station after you had got your orders in a car. What sort of car was that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Dark blue Volkswagen Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a police car or a civilian car?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Police vehicle with license plates of the Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it have "Police" written on the side?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At that time it did not say "Police" with us, it said "Milicija", but I think that there was nothing on the car that we had at the time, only the plates were other than "Police" and they had "M" as the starting character.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you started your shift and left in the police car, did the police car remain with you at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We kept it throughout the shift, since we had a radio station in the vehicle, in the car, and we maintained contact with the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of the shift what happened to the police car?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Our shift had that one car which meant that the moment we would leave the shift, we would take that car back to the public security station, and those two from the civilian police would stay at the checkpoint, and then we would turn over the car in front of the police station. That was my duty, but at the same time my two colleagues -- I would bring there my two colleagues and then the next shift would take over this car and go over, and this whole procedure lasted for about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it possible for either you or Dusko Tadic to take that car away and use it for your own purposes when you were on duty at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Nothing like that was possible for several reasons. To begin with, we were reserve force of the police and, therefore, our possibilities were somewhat limited.
