Secondly, we had to take note of the mileage, and you could not avoid it, and you have to justify every kilometre that we passed, including those six kilometres to the police station. We had to submit all the bills, all the receipts. We could not pass any decisions on our own without the consent of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of your shift when you returned to Prijedor police station, could one of you take the car away for your own purposes?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: How could one use it for one's own purposes when it returned with the next shift to the checkpoint? The vehicle was not there. The vehicle was always at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were working with Dusko Tadic at checkpoint Orlovci, do you know where he was living?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do. He had then been given an apartment to use at Pecani. These are some apartment blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that in Prijedor, Pecani?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. What do you call it, it is a new part of that town. Pecani is some 300 or 400 metres away from the SUP, as the crow flies, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to where you lived during this time, did the police keep records of where you were staying and what your accommodation was?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you live at this time in a house in Prijedor where you had always lived or had lived for some time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were off duty, were you able to leave that house without permission of your Commander?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We had to be at home and not to go away, that is, any distance or to be simply away because we had to be on call, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you were off duty, could you have travelled around the countryside outside Prijedor without permission?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, at that time nobody could go anywhere without permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Commander, Djuro Prpos, who was in charge of the traffic police, did he keep checks on your duties? Did he check that you were at your post at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Sure he did, and we never knew when he would do that. Sometimes he would come two or three times a day, and other colleagues who were with the police, when they would pass through that checkpoint, if there were some irregularities, if I may call it that, would report to him about that. I do not know how to make it clearer to you. Everybody was involved simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you find out which shift you would be on for each day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The room in front of Djuro Prpos's office had the schedule on the wall hanging with our shifts, and we ourselves after a few days already knew which shift we would be on because we knew for how long we were supposed to be at work and how long we could rest, although, as I say, there was a schedule, there was a plan of work, hanging on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The schedule that was hanging on the wall, did that give the information about where you would be on duty and what time that would be and who was in the Unit?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that schedule prepared from the office which was used by Djuro Prpos for the administration of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I guess so. I did not check that, but since he issued all the orders he must have been the one who also went through that schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said you were mobilized in May. Was that the same year as the conflict in Kozarac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Let me think, I have to remember. It was when we took over the power in Prijedor. I would not know exactly, but that was, yes, that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You date that year from the time that power was taken over in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By the power in Prijedor, do you mean when the municipality and the Crisis Staff was formed for the running of opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to power being taken over in Prijedor. What do you mean by that? Perhaps you can explain it in your own words?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do not know. Perhaps we use the term which is not quite adequate, but that is when the Serbs took over the power in Prijedor because that was the largest Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you work in the reserve police from Prijedor police station? You told us you started in May. When did you finish working?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think sometime towards the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you started your mobilization in the reserve police at Prijedor in May 1992, how long after that was it that you came to checkpoint Orlovci to work there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I would not know. I could not be very exact, perhaps a month or a month and a half. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic you first met when you went to work at that checkpoint. Did you meet him at the police station for the first time, or did you meet him actually at the checkpoint for the first time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, naturally in the police station and then we went to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst you were working with him at checkpoint Orlovci, can you think of any times when he absented himself for any long periods from his post there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Something like that could not happen, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whilst you were on duty with him at checkpoint Orlovci, did you talk to him about other matters other than the police work that you were involved with at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, we usually talked about business, about work and everyday things, nothing else. Why should we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was his behaviour and character like at this time when you were working with him for those months?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: His behaviour was quite normal. We got along very well, all three of us, and that is something which we agreed on the first day and that is how we did everything. We always agreed, we always reached an understanding. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he expressing any extreme views to you about nationalist politics or anti-Muslim feelings?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see socialise with him after work when you were off duty?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, even though there was very little time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever come across him when you were off duty and he was off duty in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Very seldom, perhaps only when I went out shopping to buy something for my family, but not that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember when you finished working at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think it was in the beginning of August. I cannot remember exactly, but it could have been three or four days after Dusko Tadic left the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When Dusko Tadic left the checkpoint, do you know where else he went to work?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I cannot be quite sure, but from what I heard -- as a matter of fact, I met him once in the town and we chatted for a while and I learned that he went to Kozarac to work, but I do not know whether that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know what time that was you had that conversation with him, how long after the time that he had finished working with you at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Why, I think it must have been a day or two later when we met in town, so I asked him what he was doing, how he was doing and like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The third member of your Unit, Miroslav Cvijic, did he continue working with you at checkpoint Orlovci for those two or three days after Dusko Tadic had left?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Cvijic was the first one to leave the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your duties after you had finished at checkpoint Orlovci, where did you go to work after that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I continued to be on the reserve civilian police. I was on duty in town in front of the Balkan hotel in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: For about a month, perhaps a little longer. After that I was under directives of labour and I went back to the company where I worked, where I had worked before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were records kept of the hours of shifts that you worked at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, the shift Commander had it. After I would go to him and reported that the whole shift had arrived. I would be given the keys of the official car and he would note it down, and I would leave the office and go to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know in what document he noted down when you reported for your shift?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was a large green notebook, thickish and it had already printed room for columns and things to write in schedules and times and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were the other shifts of the traffic police also listed in this book?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Of course, all the shifts were in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the pages of that document would contain the names of other policemen, other than the three of you working at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether the Commander recorded in the same book or not, but we all had the same obligation to report. Whether there was one book for per checkpoint or different books for checkpoints, I do not know. I know only about the one where he recorded our shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any other documents that you were aware of that that recorded the hours that you worked as a policeman and the shifts that you worked?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: If there were or if there were not I do not know, because I had no access to these documents. Commander Duro Prpos would know it better because after I would take up duty I would simply take the keys and leave. I never stayed in that office long, never longer than five or 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to look at a document here. This is one that was served on the Prosecution much earlier in the year, your Honour, it is for June '92. I would like you to look at the document which I tender before the Court as D63A.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which is the number? Is there a number on the one that was given to the Prosecutor or do you have it before you, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It did have the computer code for the monitor of A/-2/-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe we are talking about the same document. If it would be possible to take a quick look at the document before the witness has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please show the Prosecution. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brdar, this is a photocopy from the pages of a book. I would like you to tell me if you recognise, not the information on the pages, but the book from this copy?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think this is the book that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By "this book" what do you mean? What information would have been in this book?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think that the Commander noted down our presence, but how did he do it, how did he keep the book, the records, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there are copies here for your Honours because it is something that will be too indistinct to use on the overhead monitor. Translations have also been done of the same pages, your Honour. The translation here I tender before the Court as D63B. There is no need to put that in front of the witness, if the Prosecution agree, it seems pointless.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you offering 63A into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 63A I am offering into evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 63A and then we will talk about B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, for convenience purposes there is of course no objection to the translated portion being presented to the Court at this time rather than the document which is in front of the witness at this moment. However, it appears to me that the relevance and foundation of this document are in the process of being explained. I have no objection to the Court looking at the document and considering it as we proceed, but I would prefer to reserve any final objection on the document until we are concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this a part of the document -- no, you said that this and I gather the translation were given shortly after you received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document itself in Serbo-Croat was served in February of this year, not the translation. We have had that done for court purposes to assist your Honours. It is merely there for guidance and put forward as D63B.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tieger, what is your objection to 63A?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, there is no question but that the translation which is presented to the Court now will be of assistance as counsel is questioning the witness. There is no objection with respect to the timing of receipt. Nevertheless, it is my impression that both the relevance and relative foundation of this document are exactly the subject matter of the current line of enquiry, and I would like to reserve any ultimate objection on the admissibility of this document until that is concluded.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take your earphones off, please? Would you take your earphones off. (The witness removed his earphones).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather it is a schedule. Is it a schedule for everyone or is it just a schedule for he and the two other persons who worked at the checkpoint during the hours that he worked, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a schedule of working hours for Dusko Tadic. This witness is not included on the page. There are numbers on the page and Tadic happens to be No. 45. Elsewhere in the book this witness would have been found. We have had only access to it in the form that we can present it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it is a schedule for Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This I gather from listening to the witness was prepared by the Shift Commander, if the Shift Commander did for Mr. Tadic what he did for him. I am sure there would no reason why he would not. I suppose, I do not know, that is what the Prosecutor would argue. The Shift Commander, though, he is not one of the three witnesses? Is he one of the three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Duro Prpos, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I guess we had talked about that in camera. Perhaps we can talk about that because he still may be coming as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not coming, your Honour. We have had no response to our enquiries.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I said. The letter was sent. We can talk about it in closed to see whether there is any response. What I would like to find out is the status of him as a witness. We will stand in recess now. Is there anything else that either one wants to say about this document and about the objection so that we can consider it over the noon recess, unless the parties can reach some agreement? Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I just want to make it clear that it is not the Prosecution's intention to place unreasonable obstacles in front of the admissibility of any document, particularly in the light of the known complications surrounding obtaining documents. Nevertheless, I was in a position, and remain in a position I think, to evaluate the aspects of this document relative to its admissibility at what struck me as a fairly early stage. The point being that we may be able to resolve it over the recess. It may well be that this witness or the representations of counsel can obviate any potential problems foreseen by the Prosecution. My only concern was based on the information I had available at this stage of the examination, I had concerns about what this document meant and where it might be going. So it might not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kay, this is the document that you gave in early February?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In Serbo-Croat. The translation you have not given at all, but you do have a copy for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You might give that to the Prosector over the lunch recess as well and the two of you can talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sure they have had it translated already, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As many problems as we have had with translation, maybe we need a copy of theirs and a copy of your translation and then we can put them together and see how different they are. I think they should have a copy of whatever we are looking at, that is my only point, but that is easy to resolve. The two of you get together, see if you can work it out. I am very much interested in receiving as much evidence as possible. We try not to apply technical rules. So, if you can work it out then that will save the Judges having to make a ruling on it. We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding the matter relating to, what was it, 63, was it 63A, have you, lawyers, talked about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we have. The bottom line is that I think, in view of the Tribunal's Rules, the Prosecution's concerns are more a matter of the weight to be given to these documents than their admissibility. We, therefore, do not object to their tender in the fashion the Defence sought.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. We will listen to the testimony, see how it comes in and we will admit it and give it the weight appropriate. So 63A is admitted and 63B is also admitted. Are you ready for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, if Mr. Brdar could be returned to court? MIROSLAV BRDAR, recalled Examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I have just handed into the Court two documents, one a record sheet with the writing in Serbo-Croat which is D63A. It is marked "June '92". The second document is a translation of that into English, but with the records still the same. That is 63B. Your Honours will notice that date and type of duty or changes and number of hours on duty is on the top of that translation. This witness has before him solely the document in Serbo-Croat which is 63A and 63B is given to the Court for guidance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you, Mr. Kay, ask the witness to help with these numbers that are in the boxes? I am having a little difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the witness through the document. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brdar, if you could just look at that document that is in front of you, if you could unfold it? Do you see on that document the name of Tadic Dusko?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are other names in columns on that document with part of the name covered over, is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that you were aware that this document formed part of a book in Prijedor police station, is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, it is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you understand then the contents of this document to record?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think that it records the day and hour of the duty of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the column 45 for Tadic, Dusko, in June 1992 and look at the right hand of the page below 16, can you see that? Do you see in the box for 16 the figures 7 to 15 over an 8?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What would that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: This is probably the -- our shift from 7.00 to 3 o'clock in the afternoon which means an eight-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just above that there is another figure that reads "KS 760" maybe even "780". Do you know what that series of figures and letters there would indicate? You can see in the column for 17 it is rather more clearly as "KS 716". Do you know what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I would not know. I think this is some kind of code used by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move to the next box for 17th June, what are the hours recorded there of the shift?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The same as on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that 7 to 15 for eight hours?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, 7 to 15, eight hours work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 18th June, can you see what hours for the shift are recorded there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 21 which means 9 o'clock in the afternoon, in the evening, until 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many hours would that shift have been?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 10 hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that 10 hours?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is what it says here. I think it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we move now to 19th June, can we see what hours that shift would have worked on that day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Again, like on the previous day, from 21 p.m. until 7.00 in the morning, 10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to the 20th June, can we see what hours of shift are recorded there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 15 p.m. until 21, which would mean from afternoon until evening, six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 21st June, can we see what hours the shift would have been then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Identical as for the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is 1500 hours to 2100 hours for six hours?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 15 to 21, six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 22nd June, can we see what hours of shift would have been worked then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7.00 to 1500, eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And 23rd June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Again 7.00 to 1500, eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 24th June, can we see what shift hours were worked then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Again repeated, 21 p.m. until 7.00 in the morning, 10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 25th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The same again, 2100 until 7.00 in the morning, 10-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we move to 26th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Then we see again 1500 to 2100, six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 27th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Again 1500 to 2100, six hours work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 28th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 28th, 7.00 to 1500, eight-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 29th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7.00 to 1500, eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then 30th June?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2100 until 7.00 in the morning, 10-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this document there are names that have been obscured by black ink, but is it correct that this document also reflects other working hours in other shifts for other names within the book?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Do you mean from the Orlovci checkpoint or some other checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not Orlovci checkpoint, but just generally maybe other checkpoints or other duties, but other names recorded as working other periods of duty?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, yes quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you now to look at another document which is the July sheet. If this document could be, first of all, shown to Mr. Tieger and then put before the witness? (Handed). If it could be marked 64A? Mr. Brdar, could you just look at that document that has been placed before you, and tell us whether you recognise it as a similar sheet of paper for July 1992 as you were looking at for June 1992?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I have got here again in the same form a copy for each of your Honours, if they could be marked 64A for the Serbo-Croat and 64B for the English translation and there is an extra copy for Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 64A and 64B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged. Mr. Brdar, if you could look again at this document which is headed "July '92", and do you see at position 43 in the column the name "Tadic, Dusko"?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could look at this document again with us? Does it record on 1st July what hours of shift Dusko Tadic was recorded as working?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were those hours?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2100 until 7 o'clock in the morning, a 10-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2nd July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2nd July, 1500 until 2100 in the evening which means six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 3rd July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 3rd July, the same, 1500 until 21 in the evening, six hours work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 4th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 4th July, 700 to 1500, eight-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 5th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 5th July, 7 to 15 again, eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 6th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2100 until 7.00 in the morning, 10 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 8th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 700 to 1900, 12 hours work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 9th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: From 1900 until 7.00 in the morning, 12 hours again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 11th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 8.00 to 2000, 12 hours shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 12th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2000 to 8.00 in the morning, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 14th July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 15th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 1900 to 7.00 in the morning, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 17th July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 18th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 1900 to 7.00 in the morning, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 20th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7 to 1900, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 21st July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 1900 to 7.00 in the morning, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 23rd July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7 to 1900, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 24th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 1900 to 7.00 in the morning, 12-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 26th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7 to 1900, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 27th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 1900 to 7.00 in the morning, 12-hour shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 29th July?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 7 to 1900, 12 hours.
